tagline: Small language, few surprises, fast enough.
intro: Go is deliberately small — you can hold the whole language in your head — and it compiles to fast native code, so algorithmic solutions comfortably pass. The trade for DSA practice is a thin standard library: no priority queue you can just use, and until recently no generics, so you write a little more by hand than in C++ or Java. In exchange, nothing is hidden and nothing is magic.

sections.title: Setup & Program Skeleton
sections.body_md: Install Go and check `go version` — 1.21 or newer, which added the builtin `min`/`max` and the `slices`/`maps` packages that make DSA code far less verbose. Run a single file with `go run main.go`. Every file declares a package; the entry point is `func main()` in `package main`. Unused imports and unused local variables are compile ERRORS, not warnings.

sections.title: Input / Output
sections.body_md: `fmt.Scan` is convenient but slow. For competitive input use a `bufio.Scanner` split on words, and give it a large buffer — the default maximum token/line size is only 64KB and it fails silently past that. Buffer output too, with `bufio.Writer` and a deferred `Flush`.

sections.title: Types, Variables & Zero Values
sections.body_md: Every variable has a zero value — `0`, `""`, `false`, `nil` — so declarations are never uninitialised. `int` is 64-bit on modern platforms, which removes most overflow worry, though it still wraps rather than erroring. Go has NO implicit numeric conversion: mixing `int` and `int64` is a compile error, which is verbose but catches real bugs.

sections.title: Control Flow
sections.body_md: There is exactly one loop keyword: `for`. It covers the C-style loop, the while loop, the infinite loop, and iteration via `range`. `if` can declare a variable scoped to the statement, which is the idiomatic way to handle a `(value, ok)` pair. `switch` does NOT fall through by default — the opposite of C.

sections.title: Functions, Closures & defer
sections.body_md: Functions are values, so closures are the natural way to write a recursive helper that needs shared state — declare the variable first, then assign the function, or the recursive call cannot see the name. `defer` runs on function exit and is the standard way to guarantee a flush or unlock.

sections.title: Arrays, Slices & the Aliasing Trap
sections.body_md: An array has a fixed length that is part of its type; a slice is a view (pointer, length, capacity) over a backing array — and slices are what you actually use. The crucial consequence: two slices can share one backing array, so writing through one is visible through the other. `append` may or may not reallocate, which makes this intermittent and therefore easy to miss.

sections.title: Strings, Bytes & Runes
sections.body_md: A string is an immutable slice of BYTES. Indexing gives a byte; `range` gives runes (Unicode code points) along with their byte offsets. For ASCII interview input the two coincide, so it is easy to write byte-indexing code that quietly breaks on anything else. Build strings with `strings.Builder`, never `+=` in a loop.
sections.code:
import (
	"strings"
	"strconv"
)

s := "hello"
s[0]                       // byte 104, NOT "h"
string(s[0])               // "h"
len(s)                     // BYTES
len([]rune(s))             // characters

for i, r := range s {      // i is a BYTE offset; r is a rune
	_ = i
	_ = r
}

strings.Split("a,b", ",")
strings.Join([]string{"a", "b"}, "-")
strings.Contains(s, "ell")
strings.ToUpper(s)
strings.TrimSpace(s)
strings.Repeat("ab", 3)
strconv.Itoa(42)
n, _ := strconv.Atoi("42")

// Build with a Builder: strings are immutable, so += is O(n^2).
var sb strings.Builder
for i := 0; i < n; i++ {
	sb.WriteByte('a')
}
result := sb.String()

// Mutating: convert to []byte (or []rune for non-ASCII), edit, convert back.
bs := []byte(s)
bs[0] = 'H'
s = string(bs)

sections.title: Maps & Sets
sections.body_md: Maps are hash tables with O(1) average access. Two things to internalise: reading a missing key returns the zero value rather than an error (so `m[k]++` just works, but you cannot tell absent from zero without the two-value form), and iteration order is deliberately randomised so you must sort keys for deterministic output.

sections.title: Sorting, slices & container/heap
sections.body_md: The `slices` package (1.21+) is what you want: `slices.Sort`, `slices.BinarySearch`, `slices.Contains`, `slices.Reverse` — all generic, all concise. For a priority queue there is no ready-made type: `container/heap` supplies the algorithms and you implement five methods to supply the storage.

sections.title: Common Gotchas
sections.body_md: Go has fewer traps than C++ or Python, and the ones it has are mostly about slices sharing memory and nil maps. The compiler catches a surprising amount — unused variables, unused imports, missing conversions — so lean on it rather than fighting it.
